1.1. General Introduction
1. A skin sensitiser refers to a substance that will lead to an allergic response following repeated skin
contact as defined by the United Nations Globally Harmonized System of Classi fication and Labelling of
Chemicals (UN GHS) (1). There is general agreement on the key biological even ts underlying skin
sensitisation. The current knowledge of the chemical and biological mechanisms associated with skin
sensitisation initiated by covalent binding to proteins has been summarised as an Adverse Outcome
Pathway (AOP) (2) that begins with a molecular initiating event, leading to intermediate key events (KEs),
and terminating with the adverse effect, allergic contact dermatitis.
2. The skin sensitisation AOP focuses on chemicals that react with amin o acid residues (i.e. cysteine
or lysine) such as organic chemicals. In this instance, the molecular initiating event (i.e. the first KE), is the
covalent binding of electrophilic substances to nucleophilic centres in skin proteins. The second KE in this
AOP takes place in the keratinocytes and includes inflammatory responses as wel l as changes in gene
expression associated with specific cell signalling pathways such as the antioxidant/electrophile response
element (ARE)-dependent pathways. The third KE is the activation of dendritic cells, typically assessed by
expression of specific cell surface markers, chemokines and cytokines. The fourth key event is T-cell
proliferation, and the adverse outcome is presentation of allergic contact dermatitis.
3. The assessment of skin sensitisation has typically involved the use of labora tory animals. The
classical methods that use guinea pigs, the Guinea Pig Maximisation Test (GPMT ) and the Buehler Test
(OECD TG 406) (3) assess both the induction and elicitation phases of skin sensitisation. The murine tests,
such as the local lymph node assay (LLNA) (OECD TG 429) (4) and its three non-radioactive modifications
— LLNA: DA (OECD TG 442A) (5), LLNA: BrdU-ELISA, and BrdU-FCM (OECD TG 442B) (6) — all assess
the induction phase exclusively and have gained acceptance, since they provide an advantage over the
guinea pig tests in terms of animal welfare together with an objective measurement of the induction phase
of skin sensitisation.
4. Mechanistically-based in chemico and in vitro test methods (OECD TG 442C, 442D, 442E) (7, 8,
9) addressing the first three KEs of the skin sensitisation AOP can be used to evaluate the skin sensitisation
hazard potential of chemicals. With the exception of the kinetic Direct Pepti de Reactivity Assay (k-DPRA)
(TG442C), none of these test methods are considered sufficient stand-alone replacements of animal data
to conclude on the skin sensitisation potential of chemicals or to provide information for potency sub-
categorisation according to the UN GHS (sub-categories 1A and 1B). However, data generated with these
in chemico and in vitro methods addressing multiple KEs of the skin sensitisation AOP can be use d
together, as well as with information sources such as in silico and read-across predictions from chemical
analogues, within integrated approaches to testing and assessment (IATA) or defined approaches (DAs).
Results from the individual information sources can only be used in DAs if the substances fall within the
applicability domains of the methods, which are described in the “Initial Considerations, Applicability and
Limitations” sections of the respective methods (TG 442C, Appendices I -II; TG 442D, Appendices IA-IC;
TG 442E Annexes 1-4) (7, 8, 9), and in Appendices I-V of this guideline for the in silico information sources.

5. Results from multiple information sources can be used together in DAs to achieve an equi valent
or better predictive capacity than that of the animal tests to predict responses in humans. A DA consists of
a fixed data interpretation procedure (DIP) (e.g. a mathematical model, a rule-based approach) applied to
data (e.g. in silico predictions, in chemico, in vitro data) generated with a defined set of information sources
to derive a prediction without the need for expert judgment. Individual DAs for skin sensitisation and their
respective information sources were originally described in Guidance Document 256, Annex I/II (10) and a
preliminary assessment was published in Kleinstreuer et al (11). The DAs use method combinations
intended to overcome some of the limitations of the individual methods to provide increased confidence in
the overall result obtained. The ultimate goal of DAs is to provide information t hat is equivalent to that
provided by animal studies, i.e. information that can be used for hazard identification, potency (sub)-
categorisation, and/or a quantitative measure of sensitisation potency, used to derive a point of departure
(PoD).
6. Testing laboratories should consider all relevant available information on the test chemical prior to
conducting the studies as directed by a DA. All available information could include, for example, the identity
and chemical structure of the test chemical and its physicochemical properties. Such information should
be considered in order to determine whether the individual OECD test guideline methods and any in silico
information source used under a specific DA are applicable for the test chemical.
7. When performing a hazard evaluation, potency (sub)-categorisation, and/or PoD pred iction based
on the output from an in vivo (e.g. LLNA) test, an in chemico test, an in vitro test, an in silico approach, a
DA, or any combination thereof, the same principles always apply. That is, all available information relevant
to the chemical in question as well as toxicological data on structurally related test chemi cals, if available,
should be taken into consideration.
8. This Guideline was developed with the input of an OECD Expert Group on Defined Approaches for
Skin Sensitisation (EG DASS) comprised of scientific experts from regulatory agencies, validation bodies,
non-governmental organisations, and industry.
9. Multiple rule-based DAs are included in this Guideline and are described in the context of their primary
intended regulatory purpose: hazard identification, i.e. discrimination between skin sensitisers and non-
sensitisers (Part I), potency sub-categorisation (Part II), or derivation of a point of departure (Part III)1. The
DA included in Part II is also suitable for hazard identification (Part I). The DA(s) included in Part III cannot
be used in Part I or Part II unless mentioned specifically for their use. The evaluation and review of the DAs
are described in detail in the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for
Skin Sensitisation (12).
10. A comprehensive dataset of 196 chemicals with DA predictions, data on individual information
sources, highly curated LLNA and Human Patch Predictive Test (HPPT) dat a, and physicochemical
properties, was compiled and is attached as Annex 2 to the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL)
on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (12). Information on the curation of this data is detailed
in Annexes 3 and 4 of the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for
Skin Sensitisation (12). Out of the 196 chemicals, 168 chemicals have classifications based on LLNA data
and 66 chemicals have classifications based on human data, which were all agreed upon by the EG DASS
and used to evaluate the performance of the DAs when using the initially included (see paragraph 11) test
methods and in silico models. Due to the availability of data, this dataset contains mainly cosme tic
ingredients but also other types of chemicals that are used across sectors such as preservatives, dyes, or
food ingredients. The dataset is chemically diverse as shown by the range of physi cochemical properties
covered by these chemicals: it contains small and large molecules (molecular weig ht ranges from 30 to

512 g/mol), hydrophilic and hydrophobic substances (Log P ranges from -3.9 to 9.4) , liquids and solids
(melting point ranges from -122 to 253 ºC), volatile and non-volatile substances (boiling point ranges from -
19 to 445 ºC). Further details on the chemical space characterization of the reference database are
available in Section 4 of the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for
Skin Sensitisation (12).
11. This Guideline, when initially adopted, included DAs developed to be performed with a specific set
of methods, i.e. the Direct Peptide Reactivity Assay (DPRA), KeratinoSens ™, and the Human Cell Line
Activation Test (h-CLAT), for the “2 out of 3” approach (2o3), and DPRA, h-CLAT, and either Derek Nexus
or OECD quantitative structure-activity relationship ((Q)SAR) Toolbox for the i ntegrated testing strategy
(ITS). These DAs are referred as ‘classic DAs’ together or ‘classic 2o3 DA’ and ‘classic ITS DA’ throughout
this Guideline. In the course of evaluating and developing the first DAs and specific infor mation
sources, a number of analyses were conducted by the EG DASS members. These includ e the
drafting of an evaluation framework for each DA, building, curating, and characterising chemical
reference lists of human and murine data, and developing decision trees and other tools to
incorporate in silico information sources into the relevant DAs and guideline. The group also
identified sources of uncertainty and potential limitations of the DAs and information sources, as
well as borderline test results, and assessed the impact of these on the performance of the DAs.
These analyses are specific to the creation of the original DASS guideline an d information
sources published in 2021 and can be found in the main document and Annexes 1 & 3-8 of the
Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation
(12).
12. In 2025, this guideline was updated to (i) include similar methods 2 to the methods (see
paragraph 11) used for the initial adoption of this guideline and (ii) to include part III on Defined
Approaches for derivation of PoD. Based on the 2025 revision, Annex 2 of the supporting
document has been updated with new performance information relevant to the new i nformation
sources and DAs that have been added to the guideline.
13. Since the original guideline adoption, other in chemico (included in TG 442C) and in vitro (included
in TGs 442D/E) methods have been proposed and inserted into this Guideline as altern ative information
sources in the DAs (see Table 1.1 and subsequent sections of this document for the list of methods
permitted for use in each DA). The performances of the DAs using the alternative information sources have
been evaluated with available datasets for each permutation and can be found in Tables 1.1-1.3 below
and in Annexes 2 and 9 of the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs)
for Skin Sensitisation (12).

content:
1.2.1 DAs in Part I and Part II.
14. The DAs currently described in Part I and Part II of this guideline are:
• The 2o3 defined approach to skin sensitisation hazard identification based on in chemico (KE1)
and in vitro (KE2/KE3) data (13, 14). See Part I.
2 Similar methods in this guideline refer to methods that targe t a same key event (KE) and/or that are based on a
similar technology.
• The integrated testing strategy (ITS) for UN GHS potency categorisation based on in chemico
(KE1) and in vitro (KE3) data, and in silico predictions (15), with a DIP developed with EG DASS
input. See Part II.
15. The DAs described in this guideline are based on the use of validated OECD test methods for
which transferability, within- and between-laboratory reproducibility have been char acterised in the
validation phase (OECD 442C/D/E, (7, 8, 9)).
16. The ITS DAs make use of well-defined in silico information sources. Information on each model,
including its description, applicability domain, and protocol to generate predic tions is available in
Appendices I- II. Additionally, key information related to the OECD Principles for the Validation , for
Regulatory Purposes, of (Q)SAR Models (16), is described in individual QSAR Mo del Reporting Format
(QMRF) documents (17).
17. All DAs described in Parts I and II of this guideline can be used to address countries' requirements
for discriminating sensitisers (i.e. UN GHS Category 1) and non- sensitisers (UN GHS Not Classified (NC)),
though they do so with different sensitivities and specificities (detailed in the respective descriptions of
each DA and in Annexes 2 and 9 of the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches
(DAs) for Skin Sensitisation) (12)).
18. The ITS DA can also be used to discriminate chemicals into three UN GHS potency categories
(Category 1A = strong sensitisers; Category 1B = other sensitisers), and NC.
19. The known limitations and applicability domains of the individual in formation sources were used
to design workflows for assigning confidence to each of the predictions produced by the DAs described in
this guideline. In order to have a high confidence prediction, the underlying data must meet criteria in the
respective in chemico/in vitro TGs (see TG 442C, Appendices I-II; TG 442D, Appendices IA-IC; TG 442E
Annexes 1-4 (7, 8, 9)); for the ITS DA, in silico predictions must fall within the applicability domain of the
model used (see Appendices I- II). DA predictions with high confidence for hazard identification and/or
potency categorisation are considered conclusive. DA predictions with low confidenc e are considered
inconclusive for hazard identification and/or potency categorisation (see Sections 2.1.4 and 3.1.4 for further
information).These inconclusive predictions may nevertheless be considered in a weight- of-evidence
approach and/or within the context of an IATA together with other information sources (e.g. demonstration
of exposure to the test system, existing in vivo data, clinical data, read-across, other in chemico/in vitro/in
silico data, etc.).
20. The performance of the classic DAs in this guideline (see paragraph 11) were evaluated us ing a
curated dataset of up to 168 test chemicals with classifications based on LLNA and up to 66 chemicals
with classifications based on human data and corresponding information source data, where available. For
additional details see Annex 3 of the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches
(DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (12). The performances of the DAs using the alternative information sources 3
have been evaluated against both LLNA and human-based reference data, according to available datasets
for each permutation, and can be found in Table 1.1 below and in Annexes 2 and 9 of the Supporting
document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (12).

1.2.2. DAs in Part III
25. The DAs currently described in Part III of this guideline are:
• The Skin Allergy Risk Assessment – Integrated Chemical Environment (SARA-ICE) defined
approach which is a Bayesian Statistical model for the derivation of a quantitative point of departure
based on in Chemico (KE1), in vitro (KE2/KE3), and/or (existing) in vivo (KE4/AO) data (4-9). See
Part III.
• The “Regression-based” Defined Approach (DA) derives a point of departure for skin sensitisation
based on quantitative (dose-response and kinetic) data from in vitro and in chemico assays
addressing KE1, KE2, and KE3 of the AOP. See Part III.
26. The SARA-ICE DA in part III allows for the use of existing in vivo data from the LLNA or from
human predictive patch tests as available; no new in vivo data should be generated for use in this DA.
6 Datasets which use all available data points for a specifi c permutation of the 2o3 or ITS DA (see Annex 9 of the
Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (12)).
27. SARA-ICE in Part III is a Bayesian statistical model which estimates a probabilistic distributi on
from which a quantitative point of departure for skin sensitisation risk assessment c an be derived. SARA-
ICE is freely available for download within a graphical user interface (LINK TO SARA-ICE APP7)
28. The SARA-ICE DA derives a point of departure for risk assessment. The model es timates the does
at which skin sensitisation is likely to occur in 1% of an eligible human populat ion (estimated dose, ED 01),
reported as a distribution with associated confidence intervals. An upper bound is imposed on ED01 values,
at a threshold of 60,000 µg cm -2. This reflects the bound for a GHS classification of NC and an implicit
assumption that the chemical under consideration for PoD based risk assessment is a sensitiser at some
exposure level. The PoD is therefore defined as the best estimate (geometric mean) of the distribution of
the ED01 truncated at 60,000 µg cm-2.
29. SARA-ICE PoDs, computed as the mean of the ED 01 distribution conditional on it being less than
60,000 µg cm -2, were compared to reference DSA1+ values 8 reported in literature (18). The reference
value is termed the median sensitization potency estimate (MSPE) and is reported as a weight-of-evidence
potency metric calculated from human data. SARA-ICE PoD estimates were computed for the 196
chemicals in the defined approaches for skin sensitisation (DASS) reference data (12) using a) NAM data
also reported in the evaluation set (single input for DPRA, KeratinoSens and h-CLAT) and b) a single
kDPRA sourced from (Natsch and Gerberick, 2022). A DSA1+ MSPE value was define d for 54 / 66
chemicals with human reference data in the DASS evaluation set. A positi ve correlation exists (Pearson
correlation coefficient is 0.64) and 46 / 54 (85%) of SARA-ICE PoDs are within 10 -fold of the reference
value. Roughly one third, 19 / 54 (35%) of SARA-ICE PoDs are within 2-fold of the reference value. SARA-
ICE PoDs, calculated in the same way as above, were also compared to 154 chemicals wi th reference
LLNA MLLPs sourced from OECD DASS reference data (12). A positive corr elation exists (Pearson
correlation coefficient is 0.71) and 122 / 154 (79%) of SARA-ICE PoDs are within 10 -fold of the reference
value. Again, roughly one third, 49 / 154 (32%) of SARA-ICE PoDs are within 2-fold of the reference value.
Figure 1.1 shows SARA-ICE PoDs compared to reference MSPEs (left) and reference LLNA MLLPs (right).
Further analyses are made in Appendix 3 of the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined

section_title: 1.3 Limitations
content:
30. The identified limitations of the DAs and their individual components are summarised below. The
limitations of the DAs are based on the limitations of the individual in chemico/in vitro/in silico information
sources. Details on the limitations of individual in chemico/in vitro and in silico information sources to
determine confidence in Part I/Part II DA predictions are provided in Sections 2.1.4 and 3.1.4 and in the
respective TGs (TG 442C, Appendices I-II; TG 442D, Appendices IA-IC; TG 442E , Annexes 1-4) (7, 8, 9)
and in Appendices I-II of this Guideline.
31. The SARA-ICE DA is intended to predict a point of departure for use in risk assessme nt, so the
performance assessment is based on quantitative regression (Figure 1 .1). More details are provided in
Part III of this Guideline, as well as in the Supporting Document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined
Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (12).
1.3.1 Limitations of individual in chemico/in vitro information sources
32. Users should refer to the limitations of the individual in chemico/in vitro test methods as specified
in their respective TGs, which are revised as new data become available and should be consulted regularly
(TG 442C, Appendices I-II; TG 442D, Appendices IA-IC; TG 442E Annexes 1-4) (7, 8, 9). The most up-to-
date published version of the respective TGs should always be used. For example, so me types of
chemicals such as metals, inorganic compounds, lipophilic subst ances, substances of unknown or variable
compositions, complex reaction products and biological materials (UVCBs) and mixtures, may not be within the
applicability domain for certain test methods. When considering testing of mixtures, di fficult-to-test
chemicals (e.g. unstable), or test chemicals not clearly within the applicabi lity domain, upfront
consideration should be given to whether the results of such testing will yield results that are meaningful
scientifically. In cases where evidence can be demonstrated on the non-applic ability of the information
source to specific categories of chemicals, the information source should not b e used for those specific
categories of chemicals.
33. Individual assay results within borderline ranges (BRs; Annex 1) may yield inconclusive 2o3 DA
predictions. The applicability of individual information sources is descr ibed in the relevant Test Guideline
(in chemico/in vitro). The consideration of limitations of individual in chemico/in vitro test methods in each
2o3 and ITS DA is detailed in Section 2.1.4 (Figure 2.1) and Section 3.1.4 (Figure 3.1).
1.3.2 Limitations of in silico information sources
34. The ITS DA includes an in silico tool as an information source. These tools can either perform
automated read-across or (Q)SAR predictions. (Q)SARs include both structure- activity relationship (SAR)
models ( i.e. structural alerts, expert systems) and quantitative structure-activity relations hip (QSAR)
models ( i.e. statistical tools). (Q)SAR models should fulfil the OECD Principles for the Validation, for
Regulatory Purposes, of (Q)SAR Models and be described in a QSAR Model Reporting Format (QMRF)
document (16, 17) 9 . One of the OECD QSAR validation principles refers to a defined domain of
applicability. The applicability domain is the response and chemical str ucture space in which the model
makes predictions with a given reliability and the applicability domain should therefore consider the
parametric, structural, mechanistic, metabolic and response space of the model. W here a DA for skin
sensitisation includes an in silico tool, users should refer to the limitations and applicability domain of the
individual in silico tool as detailed in Appendices I-II of this Guideline. Depending on the DIP, chemicals
outside the in silico model’s applicability domain may result in DA predi ctions of low confidence that are
considered inconclusive.
1.3.3 Limitations of DAs
35. For the 2o3 DA, BRs have been defined for the individual assays addressing the three KE of the
DA, in order to define areas where lower confidence may exist (for details see Section 2.1.4 and Annex 1
of this Guideline, and Section 3.3 and Annex 7 of the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on
Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation) (12). Positive and/or negative test results falling within
these BRs and/or individual assay limitations have lower confidence and may result in inconclusive 2o3
DA predictions. Inconclusive predictions are also possible for the ITS DA (for details see Section 3.1.4
(Figure 3.1) and Annex 2 of this Guideline. Inconclusive predictions are not relevant for SARA-ICE for
PoD determination as this is a continuous metric (not categorical) made upon t he assumption a chemical
is a sensitiser.
36. Inconclusive DA predictions may nevertheless be considered in a weight- of- evidence approach
and/or within the context of an IATA together with other information sources ( e.g. demonstration of
exposure to the test system, existing in vivo data, clinical data, read-across, other in vitro/in chemico/in
silico data, etc.).
37. As the available data for each method and in silico tool differ slightly, maximal common datasets
were used for each permutation to allow direct comparison to the performance of the classic DAs, i.e. 2o3
(original: DPRA, KeratinoSens™, h-CLAT) and ITS (original: DPRA, h-CLAT, Derek Nexus (ITSv1)/OECD
(Q)SAR Toolbox (ITSv2). The maximal common datasets use all available data poi nts for a specific
permutation of the DA. Beyond specific method or tool applicability domain limi tations, no notable
differences in performance among the DAs, including substitution of original with alternate information
9 The QMRF has been slightly adapted for reporting other in silico model predictions in the context of DASS. The
adapted QPRF can be found on the OECD site for spreadsheets and software associated with OECD Test Guidelines
on Health Effects: https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/testing-of-chemicals/software-test-guidelines.html
sources based on similar methods10, were noted based on specific physicochemical properties or chemical
classes. Hazard identification performance of the DAs in comparison to LLNA-based refe rence data is
broadly equivalent to that of the classic DAs. Further, for hazard, all DAs offer better performance than the
LLNA against human-based reference data. For potency, when compared against human-based reference
data, 8/10 (80%) ITS permutations have equivalent or better accuracy than the LLNA. (60%). Two ITS
permutations (Table 1.3) had lower accuracy than the LLNA when compared to human-based reference
data which was due to several underpredictions of 1A sensitisers as 1B sensitisers. These
underpredictions may be attributed to several considerations, including human-based sub-categorizations
derived from human data where the predicted sensitising dose was close to the threshold between GHS
1A and GHS 1B sub-categorizations (termed GHS 1A- in Annex 4 of the Supporting document to the
OECD Guideline 497 on Defined Approaches for Skin Sensitisation for more information on how this was
derived). This lower accuracy is specific to these ITS DA permutations only and should be taken into
consideration when selecting specific DAs to use; use of these specific iterations needs to be justified.
These underprediction cases are discussed further in Annex 9 of the Supporting document to the Guideline
(GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (1). In addition, in determining which DA to use,
the applicability domain of the substance should be the primary driver on pri oritising the selection of a
method from TG 442C-E and/or in silico supporting documentation (Appendices I-II of this Guideline). DAs
that utilise methods outside the applicability domain of the test substance are not appropriate for use.
Additional considerations in selecting a DA may be related to the ultimate regulatory need.

38. Part I of this guideline applies to Defined Approaches (DAs) that are in tended solely for hazard
identification, i.e. distinguishing between sensitisers and non-sensitisers. A summary of the DAs for hazard
identification is provided below; additional detailed information can be fou nd in the Supporting document
to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (1). Note that the ITS DAs can
also be used for hazard characterization; please see Part II for more detail.
2.1 “2 out of 3” Defined Approach
2.1.1 Summary
39. The 2 out of 3 (2o3) DA is intended for the identification of the skin sens itisation hazard of a
chemical (i.e. UN GHS Cat. 1 vs. UN GHS NC) without the use of animal testing, The data interpretati on

section_title: procedure (DIP) is currently not designed to provide information on the potency of a skin sensitiser.
content:
40. The combination of test methods included in the 2o3 DA covers at least two of the first three KEs
of the AOP leading to skin sensitisation, i.e. KE1: protein binding (OECD TG 442C) (2); KE2: keratinocyte
activation (OECD TG 442D) (3); and KE3: dendritic cell activation (OECD TG 442E) (4).
41. The DIP requires that two concordant results obtained from methods addressing at leas t two of
the first three KEs of the skin sensitisation AOP determine the final clas sification. For the classic 2o3 DA
was evaluated against a curated dataset of up to168 chemicals with LLNA-based reference data and up to
66 chemicals with human-based reference data agreed upon by the EG DASS (Annex 2 of the Supporting
Document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (1). The performance
of the DAs using the original (i.e., classic DAs) and alternative information sources has been evaluated
against both LLNA and human-based reference data, according to available datasets for each permutation,
and can be found in Tables 2.2-2.4 below and in Annexes 2 and 9 of the Supporting Document to the
Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (1). It should be noted that due to the
imbalanced nature of the reference data (higher numbers of UN GHS Cat. 1 than UN GHS N C), the
measures of balanced accuracy are more uncertain, particularly in the case of the human data comparison.
2.1.2 Data interpretation procedure
42. The DIP in the 2o3 DA is a transparent, rule-based approach requiring no expert judgment (5, 6,
7). The approach predicts skin sensitisation hazard by sequential testing, in an un defined order, in up to
three of the internationally accepted non-animal assays mapping to KE1-3. In other words, the assays are
run for two KEs, and if these assays provide consistent results, then the chemical is predicted accordingly
as skin sensitiser or non-sensitiser. If the first two assays provide discordant results, the assay for the
remaining KE is run. The overall result is based on the two concordant findings considering the confidence
of the obtained predictions as described in Section 2.1.4.
43. The performance of the 2o3 DA was found to be impacted by the consideration of BRs for each of
the methods, as described below in Section 2.1.4, and further detailed in Section 3.3 and Annex 7 of the
Supporting Document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (1). A
decision tree is provided in Figure 2.1 of Section 2.1.4 to derive predictions for the 2o3 DA, with no
modification of the 2o3 DA DIP.
2.1.3 Description and limitations of the individual information sources
44. The individual information sources in the DA are assays included in OECD KE - based TGs for skin
sensitisation (OECD TG 442C, 442D, 442E) (2, 3, 4), and the details for the individual protocols are
provided therein.
45. The following assays from those TGs have been characterised and included in the 2o3 DA.
• KE1 (Amino acid Derivative Reactivity Assay (ADRA), Direct Peptide Reactivity Assay (DPRA); TG
442C) (2): Skin sensitisers are generally electrophilic and react with the nucl eophilic moieties of
proteins. The ADRA and DPRA measure depletion of two peptides/amino acids containing either
cysteine or lysine residues due to covalent binding. Test protocols and prediction models are found
in the TG. If borderline results are obtained for peptide depletion, additional testing should be
conducted, as specified in OECD TG 442C and in Annex 1.
• KE2 (EpiSensA, LuSens, KeratinoSens ™; TG 442D) (3): Activation of keratinocytes is
demonstrated via either a) reaction of human, immortalized keratinocytes harbouring a reporte r
gene construct via the Nrf2-Keap1 pathway (KeratinoSens, LuSens), or b) quantific ation of
changes in the expression of marker genes associated with keratinocyte activation in a
reconstructed human epidermis model (EpiSensA). Test protocols and prediction models are found
in the TG. If borderline results are obtained for luciferase induction, additional t esting should be
conducted, as specified in Annex 1.
• KE3 (Genomic Allergen Rapid Detection test (GARD®Skin), Human Cell Line Acti vation Test (h-
CLAT), Interleukin-8 Reporter Gene Assay (IL-8 Luc), U937 Cell Line Acti vation Test (U-SENS);
TG 442E) (4): Activation of antigen presenting cells is characterised by eithe r a) a change in the
expression of cell surface marker(s) associated with the process of activation of mo nocytes and
DC following exposure to sensitisers (e.g. CD86, CD54; h-CLAT, U-SENS),b) changes in IL -8
expression, a cytokine associated with the activation of DC (IL-8 Luc) or c) an end-point specific
genomic biomarker signature (GARD®skin). Test protocols and prediction models are found in the
TG. If borderline results are obtained for the assays, additional testing should be conducted, as
specified in Annex 1.
46. The current limitations of individual in chemico and in vitro test methods, such as limited solubility,
are described in their respective TGs (TG 442C, Appendices I- II; TG 442D, Appendices IA-I1C; TG 442E,
Annexes 1-4) and the validation studies cited therein (2, 3, 4).
2.1.4 Confidence in the 2o3 DA predictions
47. The limitations of the in chemico and in vitro methods used in the 2o3 DA dictate whether test
results can be used to support hazard identification and are reported in their respective TGs (TG 442C,
TG 442D, TG 442E) ( e.g. for substances that do not provide conclusive results in the individual methods
due to solubility reasons) (2, 3, 4). Additionally, assay results are subject to variability (due to, for example,
minor fluctuations in cell response) and these variations increase the uncertainty of a test result especially
when close to a (classification) cut-off. In order to define areas where lower confidence in the DA results
may exist, borderline ranges (BRs) have been statistically derived for each assay addressing the three KE
of the 2o3 DA, (see Annex 1 of this document, and Section 3.3and Annex 7 of the Supporting document
to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation) (1). The specific BRs for each
assay, as derived from their respective validation study data, are summarised in Table 2.1.

48. The incorporation of BRs into the prediction models (PM) for each of the indivi dual information

49. Positive and negative test results falling within these BRs as well as inconc lusive results due to

• In case the result of one of the 2o3 DA test methods falls into the respective test method’s BR, a
2o3 DA prediction can still be made if the outcomes of the other two test methods compos ing the

BRs).
• Similarly, in case a result is obtained in one test method that is considered inconcl usive due to
limitations or the chemical falling outside the applicability domain of the me thod, a 2o3 DA
prediction can still be made if the outcomes of the other two test methods composing the 2o3 DA
are concordant and have high confidence (i.e., results falling outside of the respective BRs).

sensitisation. The in silico prediction of skin sensitisation is provided by Derek Nexus (4) or the OECD QSAR

3.1.2 Data interpretation procedure
66. The ITS DIP uses scores assigned to the quantitative results from a KE3 (3) and a K E1 assay (1),
and from an in silico tool to discriminate chemicals into UN GHS category 1A (strong sensitiser); category
1B (other sensitiser), or Not Classified (non-sensitiser) (Table 3.1).
67. The DIP was amended from the original published version of the ITS (6-7) to change the cut-off for
1A sensitisers from a score of 7 to a score of 6 to optimize the ability of the DA to detect strong sensitisers
and to extend the applicability of the ITS to chemicals for which in silico predictions cannot be generated.
The DIP was also altered from the published version in that it was originally appl ied to ECETOC
categories13, and is here applied to the UN GHS subcategories.
68. The quantitative results of the KE1 and KE3 assays are converted into a score from 0 to 3 for each
assay, as shown in Table 3.1. For the in silico prediction, a positive outcome is assigned a score of 1; a
negative outcome is assigned a score of 0. Further details on the respective protocols are available in
Annexes 1 and 2 and Appendices I- II). When these scores have been assessed, a total battery score
ranging from 0 to 7, calculated by summing the individual scores, is used to predict the sensitising potential
(hazard identification; UN GHS Cat. 1 vs. UN GHS NC) and potency (UN GHS Cat. 1A, Cat. 1B and NC).
The positive criteria for identifying skin sensitisers (UN GHS Cat. 1) are set as a total battery score of 2 or
greater. Based on the updated DIP, a total battery score is assigned into three ranks: score of 6-7 is defined
as a strong (UN GHS Cat. 1A) sensitiser; score of 2-5 as moderate/weak (UN GHS Cat. 1B ) sensitiser;
score of 1 or 0, as not classified (i.e. a non-sensitiser).

86. Part III of the Guideline includes Defined Approaches that allow for the derivatio n of a quantitative

4.1 “SARA-ICE” Defined Approach for derivation of a point of departure
4.1.1. Summary
87. The Skin Allergy Risk Assessment-Integrated Chemical Environment (SARA-ICE) DA is a
Bayesian statistical model which estimates an ED 01, which is provided as a probability distribution. The
ED01 is an estimate of a dermal dose (µg cm -2) at which there is a 1% chance of inducing sensitization
from a human predictive patch test (HPPT). The SARA-ICE DA uses a set of define d input data and
specifies a single point, computed as the geometric mean of the ED 01 distribution conditional on it being
less than 60,000 µg cm-2, which provides a point of departure (PoD) that can be applied within a quantitative
risk assessment for skin sensitisation.
88. The SARA-ICE DA is based on data from test methods from KEs 1-4 of the ad verse outcome in
the AOP. The SARA-ICE DA is based on a previously published SARA mode l which initially included 81
chemicals in the database and was subsequently expanded to 434 chemicals, l everaging chemicals
contained within the Integrated Chemical Environment (ICE, https://ice.ntp.niehs.nih. gov/, (2,3)). Further
description of the database on which SARA-ICE is trained is provided in Annex 10 of Supporting document
to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (1). Evaluation of SARA-ICE is
described in paragraph 100 and performance is described in section 4.1.4. Test methods which can be
used as input information sources include: the Direct Peptide Reactivity Assay (DPRA; OECD TG 442C ),
kinetic DPRA (kDPRA; OECD TG 442C), KeratinoSens (OECD TG 442D), the human cell line activation
test (h-CLAT; OECD TG 442E), and U-SENS (OECD TG 442E), as well as in vivo methods such as the
local lymph node assay (LLNA; OECD TG 429, OECD TG 442A, OECD TG 442B) and th e human
predictive patch test (HPPT) methods i.e., human repeat insult patch tests ( HRIPT) and human
maximization tests (HMT) (4 –10). Data in any combination from these test methods can also be used to
predict the ED01. Note that the SARA-ICE model may accept existing LLNA data and HPPT data as inputs;
however, new in vivo data should not be generated. The SARA-ICE model should be run using a minimum
of two in chemico and/or in vitro information sources based on different KEs.
89. The SARA-ICE DA was evaluated first using posterior predictive checks, whic h are recommended
for any Bayesian statistical model. Checks included a comparison of prior margi nal distributions against
posterior marginals to ensure model parameters are identifiable from the data. Th e SARA-ICE DA uses
latent variables to represent average quantities for each input type. Checks that latent variables are both
correlated with the ED 01 and their respective input data in the SARA-ICE database were performed.
Generating ED 01 estimates for chemicals not within the core SARA-ICE database requires the joint
posterior for the full database be approximated analytically. This approximation is then used as a prior
within a SARA-ICE production DA to generate ED 01 estimates for new input data. Further checks were
performed to ensure the production version returns the correct estimates. Details of these anal yses can
be found in Annex 11 of Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for
Skin Sensitisation (1). The database on which the model was evaluated is static (finalized December 2022)
and in case of subsequent version changes, it will be evaluated per OECD procedures.
4.1.2. Data Interpretation Procedure
90. The SARA-ICE DA uses a Bayesian statistical model to estimate the ED 01. A PoD is computed as
the geometric mean of the ED 01 distribution conditional on it being less than 60,000 µg cm -2. Technically,
the model can be run with no chemical-specific inputs, in which case the resul ting ED01 estimates will be
taken directly from the prior distribution. Using chemical-specific data to inf orm estimates will, for any
typical input, return an ED 01 estimate whose variance (uncertainty) is reduced relative to the prior. The
magnitude of reduction in uncertainty is a function of several factors including input type(s), input numbers,
and input concordance. To ensure an appreciable level of uncertainty reduction is achieved, a minimum
of 2 test methods per compound, covering 2 separate KEs from within OECD TG 442C, 442D, or 442E,
should be entered into the input template used to run the model ( LINK TO SARA-ICE APP16). Admissible
data types are indicated in Table 4.1 and Paragraph 88. There is no restriction to the maximum number of
stated data inputs, in type or experimental repeats, the model can include. Any available in vivo data may
also be included, but new in vivo data should not be produced to be used in this DA. Figure 4.1
demonstrates the workflow for use of SARA-ICE, and further details are provided in Appendix III of this
document.

91. The model estimates the ED 01 as a probability distribution which is typically summarized as a 90%
credible interval (the interval between the 5 th and 95th percentiles of the distribution). The variance of the
distribution is a measure of the uncertainty in the estimate and its width is dependent on the provided input
data, such as the number, type, and concordance between inputs. For the purposes of defining a P oD for
use in quantitative risk assessment for skin sensitisation, this distributio n is truncated at 60,000 µg cm -2
which is the maximum possible dose for a standard HRIPT. A PoD (geometric mean of the ED01
distribution) is then calculated as a summary statistic of the distribution. T he SARA-ICE Technical
Specification in Annex 10 of the Supporting Document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs)
for Skin Sensitisation [1] provides further detail on the SARA-ICE PoD.
4.1.3. Description and limitations of the predictive model and its information sources
92. The individual in chemico, in vitro, and in vivo information is generated using existing OECD test
guidelines (OECD TG 429, 442A, 442B, 442C, 442D, 442E [4- 10]) and the protocols detailed therein. In
the case of the kDPRA and KeratinoSens assays, commonly reported units are expressed as molar
concentrations. If these are provided as inputs, the model also requires the specification of the chemical’s
molecular weight to enable conversion to mass concentrations. Note that the SARA-ICE model may accept
existing LLNA data and HPPT data as inputs; however, new in vivo data should not be generated.
93. The following assays have been characterized and included as potential input information sources
in the SARA-ICE DA:
• Direct Peptide Reactivity Assay (DPRA; OECD TG 442C; KE1 [7]): Skin sensitise rs are generally
electrophilic and react with the nucleophilic moieties of proteins. The DPRA measures depletion of
two peptides containing either cysteine or lysine residues due to covalent binding. A test chemical
that induces mean peptide depletion of cysteine- and lysine-containing peptide above 6.38% (or in
the case of co-elution, cysteine-only depletion above 13.89%) is considered to be positive. The
SARA-ICE DA does not make use of this classification rule. Instead, the input into SARA-ICE is
the percentage depletion of both peptides. The SARA-ICE DA then determines the maxi mum
depletion of either of the peptides. Depletions less than 1% are interpreted as < 1%, whilst
depletions greater than 99% are interpreted as > 99%. It is noted that while the DPRA gravimetric
method has not been specifically evaluated for use in the SARA- ICE DA, given that the DPRA
gravimetric evaluation that was conducted under OECD TG 442C found that the approac hes are
equivalent, it is expected to provide data within an acceptable range for use as an input into SARA-
ICE.
• Kinetic Direct Peptide Reactivity Assay (kDPRA; OECD TG 442C; KE1 [7]): The kDPRA is intended
to quantify the reactivity of test chemicals in a time and concentration dependent manner. The rate
of depletion of the cysteine peptide (used within the DPRA) is determined. Kinet ic rate constants
are calculated and reported as the log Kmax value with Kmax having units M -1 s-1. The kDPRA is
used in the discrimination of UN GHS subcategory 1A from those not categorized as sub-category
1A. For SARA-ICE, the log Kmax is converted to units g L-1 s-1 and multiplied by -1 (such that higher
potency chemicals are associated with lower values). This is handled by the model, assumi ng the
molecular weight of the chemical has been specified. If the reactivity rate is too slow to measure,
then the input should be < X where X is the limit of detection of the test. For training purposes, this
has been assumed to be -3.5 M -1 s -1, thus, for chemicals exhibiting negligible reactivity in the
kDPRA, the input should be <-3.5.
• KeratinoSens: (In vitro Skin Sensitisation: ARE-Nrf2 Luciferase Test Method; OECD TG 442D; KE2
[6]): Keratinocytes harbouring a reporter gene construct react to possible sensitisers via the Nrf2-
Keap1 pathway. A test chemical that causes > 1.5 fold luciferase induction, at viabilities > 70%
when compared to the vehicle control, is considered to be positive. The SARA-ICE input is the
EC1.5 (µM) and the IC 50 (µM). These are converted by the template to units of µg mL -1, assuming
molecular weight has been provided. The model also accepts inputs as > X or < X where X is a
test concentration within the assay. This is required, for example, to input a ne gative test into the
model (for which no EC1.5 is defined). If the test is negative, then no luciferase induction occurs at
any test concentration and the input into the model should > X where X is the maxi mum tested
concentration. Similarly, if > 1.5 fold induction is observed at all test concentrations (i.e., the test is
positive at all test concentrations), the input into SARA-ICE should be provide d as < X where X is
the minimum test concentration.
• Human Cell Line Activation Test (h-CLAT; OECD TG442E; KE3 [4]): Activation of antigen
presenting cells is characterized by the up-regulation of CD86 and/or CD54. The h-C LAT is
considered to be positive if CD86 induction exceeds 1.5 fold and/or CD54 exceeds 2 fold at
viabilities > 50% when compared to the vehicle control. The SARA-ICE input i s both the CD54
EC200 and the CD86 EC150 (µg mL -1) and the CV75 (µg mL -1). If either value is not reported
because no change in the biomarker was observed, the input is > X where X is the maximum
concentration tested. In the case that induction exceeds thresholds at all test concentr ations for
either biomarker (i.e., the test is positive for that biomarker at all test concen trations), the model
may also accept < X where X is the minimum test concentration.
• U-SENS (OECD TG 442E; KE3 [4]): Activation of antigen presenting cells is characterised by the
up-regulation of CD86. The U-SENS is considered positive if the CD86 induction exceeds 1.5-fold
at viabilities > 70% compared to vehicle control. The SARA-ICE input is the CD86 EC150 (µg mL -
1) and CV70 (µg mL-1). If the test is negative, the input to the model is > X where X is the maximum
concentration should be used. In the event that CD86 induction exceeds the 1.5-fold at al l test
concentrations, the input should be < X where X is the minimum test concentration.
• Local Lymph Node Assay (LLNA; OECD TG429, 442A, 442B; KE4 [5,8,9]): The induc tion phase
of skin sensitization (KE4) is characterized by lymphocyte proliferation in the lymph nodes draining
the site of the exposure and is proportional to the dose and potency of the substance. The LLN A
measures proliferation relative to the vehicle control treated group for mice exposed on their ear to
a test substance of interest. The ratio of the mean proliferation for each treatment group compared
to the vehicle control is the Stimulation Index (SI). An SI ≥ 3 is considered to be indicative of skin
sensitization. The input for SARA-ICE template is the EC3 expressed as a perc ent. These are
converted to µg cm -2 by the model. The model may also accept an input for negative tests
expressed as > X where X is the maximum tested concentration. Alternatively, i f all test
concentrations result in an SI greater than 3, the recommended input into SARA-ICE is < X where
X is the lowest concentration tested. This also allows single-dose LLNA s tudies to be input in th e
SARA-ICE DA. If a single-dose LLNA is run at concentration X and the SI < 3, then the input into
SARA-ICE is > X. Conversely, if the SI > 3, the study result can be entered as < X. Only existing
LLNA data are recommended for use in the SARA-ICE model.
• Human Predictive Patch Test (HPPT [10]): HPPT methods include the human maximization test
(HMT) and the human repeat insult patch test (HRIPT). Both test methods quantify an empi rical
sensitization rate following exposure to a (potential) allergen at some chos en dermal dose. The
HMT incorporates a pre-treatment with an irritant and typically has a smaller test pool than HRIPT.
Required HPPT inputs into the SARA-ICE DA are the dermal dose expressed as µg cm-2, the total
number of test subjects and the total number of subjects sensitized following the challenge.
94. The current limitations of the individual test methods, such as with respect to solubility, are
described in the respective test guidelines and the validation studies c ited therein. No filtering of assay
data was performed prior to training the SARA-ICE DA, therefore uncertainty measures provided by the
DA should reflect such limitations. However, caution is advised when selecting inputs since biases may
nevertheless occur (e.g., when using a DPRA input for a chemical whose sensitization potential is
enhanced via metabolic activation). Only valid assay results, i.e. results wit hin the applicability domain of
each assay used as input, should be used to run the DA for regulatory purposes. Evaluation of data quality
should be made prior to use in the DA, this includes use of human data for which Stric kland et al., 2023
[10] can be used for reference.
4.1.4. Confidence in the SARA-ICE DA predictions
95. The SARA-ICE DA is built upon a Bayesian statistical model and as such provides potency
estimates with a numerical measure of precision. The provided distribution represents the r ange of ED 01
values that are both consistent with user-specified input data and the model – where the model is a
characterization of the association between ED 01 estimates and assay data for a training set of 434
chemicals. Further information on the SARA-ICE database can be found in the T echnical Specification in
Appendix 2. A decision on whether to use specific source data is dictated by the limitations of the different
input methods found within the Annex of the requisite test method (TG 429, TG 442A, TG 442B, TG 442C,
TG 442D, TG 442E). As indicated, for a higher confidence estimate, at least 2 methods that cover 2 key
events should be used as input data. A greater number of data inputs will likely a lso increase confidence
(e.g. decrease the width of the distribution) of the model ED01 output depending on the concordance of the
additional data utilized [3]. All available high-quality data is encouraged to be used.
96. A number of basic model checks were carried out to ensure that the SARA-ICE mode l is behaving
as expected. Posterior predictive checks show that the marginal posterior distributi on of each parameter
is not concentrating in the extreme tail of the prior, indicating that the chosen prior is only weakly informative
on the posterior estimate. Therefore, estimates of model parameters would be unlikel y to change if prior
choices were relaxed. Further checks were completed to confirm the model as sumption that there is a
linear relationship with non-zero slope to the predictors included in the model. Figure 4.2 shows that each
of the possible inputs is informative towards estimation of the ED 01. Further analysis shows that location-
like latent variables for each predictor are both correlated with the ED 01 and experimental repeats for
chemical. The SARA-ICE Technical Specification in Annex 10 of the Supporting Document to the
Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches (DAs) for Skin Sensitisation [1] provides a detailed explanation of
the basic model checks carried out.

in chemico and in vitro information sources (KE1, KE2, KE3) are defined in the respective guidelines

4.1.6. Predictive Capacity of the SARA-ICE DA
98. SARA-ICE derives a point of departure for risk assessment. The model estima tes the dose at
which skin sensitisation is likely to occur in 1% of an HPPT-eligible human population (ED01), reported as
a distribution with associated confidence intervals. For PoD estimation, an upper bound is imposed on the
ED01 distribution at a threshold of 60,000 µg cm -2. This reflects the bound for a GHS classification of NC
and encodes an implicit assumption that the chemical under consideration for PoD based risk assessment
is a sensitiser. The PoD is therefore defined as the geometric mean of the distribut ion of the ED 01
conditional on the ED01 being less than 60,000 µg cm-2.
99. PoDs were computed for all 196 chemicals in the DASS evaluation set (Annex 2) using a) in
chemico and in vitro data also reported in the evaluation set (which consists of a single input for DPRA,
KeratinoSens and h-CLAT) and b) a single kDPRA sourced from Natsch et al., 202 2 [12], if available). It
should be noted that 187 / 196 (95%) of chemicals in the DASS evaluation set are presented in the SARA-
ICE database. However, the data used for training versus evaluation differs for most chemicals. For training
purposes, a chemical may have both in vivo and in vitro data with multiple studies per data type. For
evaluation, inputs are restricted to a single DPRA, single KeratinoSens, single h-CLAT and, if available, a
single kDPRA study. It follows that ED 01 estimates obtained during training may be considerably different
from those obtained in the evaluation.
100. SARA-ICE PoDs, were compared to reference DSA1+ values reported in Herzler et al., 2024 [11].
The reference value is termed the median sensitization potency estimate (MSPE) and is reported as
weight-of-evidence potency metric calculated from human data. A DSA1+ MSPE value was defined for 54
/ 196 chemicals in the DASS evaluation set. A positive correlation exists (Pearson correlation coefficient
is 0.64) and 46 / 54 (85%) of SARA-ICE PoDs are within 10-fold of the reference value. Roughly one third,
19 / 54 (35%) of SARA-ICE PoDs are within 2-fold of the reference value. The same SARA-ICE PoDs were
also compared to 154 chemicals with reference LLNA MLLPs sourced from OECD DASS reference list [1].
A positive correlation exists (Pearson correlation coefficient is 0.71) and 122 / 154 (79%) of SARA-ICE
PoDs are within 10-fold of the reference value. Again, roughly one third, 49 / 154 (32%) of SARA-ICE PoDs
are within 2-fold of the reference value. SARA-ICE PoDs exhibit almost no bias relative to human reference
values (mean and median fold-differences are 1.1). Relative to LLNA reference values, the SARA-ICE PoD
is nearly 2-fold lower, on average. These comparisons are presented in Figure 1.1, section 1.2. Further
analysis was conducted based upon fewer inputs, no appreciable difference in predic tion bias was
observed for the minimum input requirement of two separate key event-based model in puts. Further
analyses are made in Annex 11 of the Supporting document to the Guideline (GL) on Defined Approaches
(DAs) for Skin Sensitisation (1).

101. The reporting of the SARA-ICE DA should follow the template described in OECD GD 255 [13],
and should include at a minimum the following elements:
• Test chemical identification ( e.g. chemical name, structural formula, composition, isomers,
impurities including their quantities as available, CAS number, batch and lot nu mber, and other

4.2 “Regression-based” Defined Approach for derivation of a point of departure
for skin sensitization
4.2.1 Summary
102. The regression-based defined approach ( DA) is based on multiple linear regression models. As
input data, quantitative (dose-response and kinetic) data from in vitro and in chemico assays addressing
KE1, KE2 and KE3 of the AOP are used. Different models were trained on (i) EC3 values from the Local
Lymph Node Assay (LLNA) [1, 2] and (ii) on weight- of-evidence (WoE) Potency Values (PV) [3] derived
from human DSA04 and NOEL values and LLNA EC3 values [4]. These individual regression models are
combined in the DA to provide a finite point of departure (PoD) that can be appli ed within a quantitative
risk assessment for skin sensitisation [5]. The PoD is both expressed as a value in % in a vehicle applied
at 25 mg/cm2 to the skin (similar to the LLNA) or as a dose per unit metric in µg/cm2. The conversion factor
between these two metrics is a fixed factor of 250.
103. The details of the training of the regression models and the set of chemica ls used are described
in detail in the open access literature [1-3]. The database with all the input data and the prediction of the
PoD for all chemicals tested (n = 220) is provided in Annex 12.a of Supporting Document to this document.
The specific test methods in the KE-based test guidelines which can be used as input information sources
include: the kinetic DPRA (kDPRA; OECD TG 442C), KeratinoSens (KS; OECD TG 442D) and the human
cell line activation test (h-CLAT; OECD TG 442E) [6-8]. Data from at least two of these information sources
are required to predict the PoD. For chemicals, which are rated as sensitisers according to a DA described
in Part I or Part II of this guideline, the input data shall include quantitative results from at least two positive
KE outcomes, whereby the kDPRA is conducted as a quantitative test for KE1 in case of a positive DPRA.
For chemicals positive in DPRA and KS, data from at least kDPRA and KS sha ll be used. For chemicals
positive in DPRA and h-CLAT, data from at least kDPRA and h-CLAT shall be used. For chemicals positive
in KS and h-CLAT, at least these data shall be used. For chemicals tested in all three KE tests and positive
in at least two tests, all available evidence including the kDPRA result shall be used, see Figure 4.3. In
addition, vapour pressure is used to correct for volatility under topical application. Evaluation of predictivity
of the DA is described in section 4.2.6.
4.2.2 Data Interpretation Procedure
104. The regression models use logarithmically transformed and normalised data from the individual
information sources and the input parameters as summarised in Table 4.2. The models combine these
data in linear regression equations with coefficients trained on the full da taset. These calculations are
made in a fully transparent spreadsheet which is provided as Annex 12.b of the Supporting Document to
this guideline [11]. The measured parameters summarised in Table 4.2 can be directly entered into the
spreadsheet to arrive at a conclusion. Depending on the available input data, multiple predictions are
made: (i) Equations EQ1, EQ4, EQ5 and EQ6 were trained against LLNA data (see [1]), while (ii) EQ1d,
EQ4d, EQ6d and EQ5e were trained against the PV (see [3]). The DA then automatically selects,
depending on the KE covered by the input data, a PoD according to the workflow in Figu re 4.3 below,
taking the more conservative estimate from the two models trained on either LLNA EC3 or PV values.
Figure 4.3. Use of the published predictive equations based on different combinations of input
data.
The DA uses the appropriate model depending on which tests are available. A conservative choice is made, taking
the lower of the two values from either (i) the models trained on LLNA EC3 values (EQ1, EQ4, EQ6 and EQ5; see
[1]) or (ii) trained on the PV values (EQ1d, EQ4d, EQ6d and EQ5e; see [3]).

4.2.3 Description and limitations of the predictive model and its information sources
106. The individual in chemico, in vitro, and in vivo information is generated using existing OECD test
guidelines (OECD TG 442C, 442D, 442E [6-8].) and the protocols detailed therein. In the case of the
kDPRA and the KeratinoSens assays, commonly reported units are expressed as molar concentrations.
The model requires the specification of the chemical’s molecular weight to ena ble conversion to mass
concentrations. In case the molecular weight is unknown (mixtures and multi-constitue nt substances of
unknown composition (i.e. UVCB substances of unknown or variable composition, complex reaction
products or biological materials), a default molecular weight of 200 g/mol can be us ed as applied in the
gravimetric DPRA (442C). This default molecular weight is also used in the gravi metric KeratinoSens
prediction model (442D). The regression-based DA can be run using data from a minimum of two KE-
based in chemico and/or in vitro information sources applicable to a particular chemical. Applicability
domain limitations as outlined in TG442c, 442d and 442e for a particular chemical may guide which assay
is being conducted. If a chemical is rated as a sensitizer due to at least two pos itive test results in TG
442C, 442D, 442E, at least the data from two positive KE shall be usedwhereby the kDPR A is conducted
as a quantitative test for KE1 in case of a positive DPRA. For chemicals po sitive in DPRA and KS, data
from at least kDPRA and KS shall be used. For chemicals positive in DPRA and h-CLAT, data from at least
kDPRA and h-CLAT shall be used. For chemicals positive in KS and h-CLAT, at least these data shall be
used. For chemicals tested in all three KE tests and positive in at least two tests, all available evidence
including the kDPRA result shall be used, see Figure 4.3. For chemicals for w hich the kDPRA is not
applicable, potency is assessed by a combination of KS and h-Clat. For details on the underlying rationale
and for possible testing schemes see [2]. All the test methods used for the reg ression DA are technically
applicable to test mixtures and considerations of the different test methods w hen using a gravimetric
approach should be followed. When assessing mixtures and no experimental vapor pressure is known,
the vapor pressure is set to zero. This is a conservative approach as the actual v apor pressure can only
reduce the predicted sensitization potency. The models have been trained on the three specific KE-based
tests and using large sets of dose- response data. If for other KE-based tests such quantitative datasets
are available, similar regression-based models may be derived in the future in analogy to [1, 2]. However,
these would need completely independent validation and assessment for predictivity and the development
of an independent calculation worksheet. Therefore, currently the DA is only appl icable to the prescribed
methods.
107. The following assays have been characterized and included as input information sources in the
regression-based DA:
• Kinetic Direct Peptide Reactivity Assay (kDPRA; OECD TG 442C; KE1 [7]): The kDPRA is intended
to quantify the reactivity of test chemicals in a time and concentration dependent manner. The rate
of depletion of the cysteine peptide (used within the DPRA) is determined. Kinet ic rate constants
are calculated and reported as the Log kmax value with kmax having units M-1 s-1. For chemicals with
no measurable reactivity above the threshold in the kDPRA, the limit vale of the Log k max = -3.5 is
entered into the model as specified in the Spreadsheet in Annex 12.b of Supporting Document to
this guideline [11]. For chemicals with a high reactivity at the earliest time point measured (10 min
in the standard setting of the kDPRA), testing at shorter incubation times should be considered in
order to not underestimate potency (as indicated in TG442C, ANNEX III, para 18).
• KeratinoSens: (In vitro Skin Sensitisation: ARE-Nrf2 Luciferase Test Method; OECD TG 442D;
KE2[6]): Keratinocytes harbouring a reporter gene construct react to possible sensitisers vi a the
Nrf2-Keap1 pathway. A test chemical that causes > 1.5-fold luciferase induction, at viabilities >
70% when compared to the vehicle control, is considered to be positive. The mod el input is the
EC1.5 (µM) and the IC50 (µM). For chemicals with no defined molecular weight, these can be entered
in µg mL-1. If no luciferase induction is observed at any test concentration (i.e., the test is negative),
the input into the model should be 4000 µM (or 800 µg mL -1), i.e. twice the maximal concentration
tested. The same approach applies to the IC50 value in case no cytotoxicity is observed as specified
in the Spreadsheet in Annex 12.b of Supporting Document to this guideline [11].
• Human Cell Line Activation Test (h-CLAT; OECD TG442E; KE3 [8]): Activati on of antigen
presenting cells is characterized by the up-regulation of CD86 and/or CD54. The h-C LAT is
considered to be positive if CD86 induction exceeds 1.5-fold and/or CD54 excee ds 2-fold at
viabilities > 50% when compared to the vehicle control. The model input is both the CD54 EC200
and the CD86 EC150 (µg mL-1) and the CV75 (µg mL-1). If either value is not reported because no
change in the biomarker was observed or cytotoxicity is observed at the maximal test
concentration, the input is 5000 µg mL-1.
108. If multiple test results are available for a given test, they are assessed for their v alidity based on
the criteria laid out in the KE-based test guidelines. If multiple valid an d concordant results are available,
the geometric mean of the individual parameters from multiple tests is used in the calculation spreadsheet.
In cases where multiple positive and negative results are available for a given KE-event based test, the
geometric mean of the data from the positive tests is used.
109. The current limitations of individual in chemico and in vitro test methods, such as limitations with
respect to solubility, are described in the respective test guidelines (TG 442C, Appendix 1; TG 442D,
Appendix 1A; TG 442E, Annex 1) and the validation studies cited therein (2, 3, 4). No filtering of assay
data to exclude chemicals outside of the application domain was performed prior to training the regression
models, therefore uncertainty measures provided by the DA should reflect such limitations. Specifically, (i)
data for chemicals falling into the borderline range of the individual methods were still used and (ii) h-CLAT
data were used independently of the cLogP of the test chemical when the models were trained. However,
caution is advised when selecting inputs since biases may nevertheless occur (e.g., when using a kDPRA
input for a chemical whose sensitisation potential is enhanced via metabo lic or abiotic activation, or for
using the kDPRA for chemicals which are predominantly reacting with amine groups as shown e.g. by the
reaction with the Lysine peptide in the DPRA; limitations of the kDPRA are summarised in TG442C,
APPENDIX III, ANNEX 1). Therefore, only valid assay results, i.e. results within the applicability domain of
each assay, should be used to run the DA for regulatory purposes. Evaluation of da ta quality should be
made prior to use in the DA.
4.2.4 Confidence in the regression-based DA predictions
110. The regression equations were built upon a training set of n = 139 - 203 chemicals. Further
information on the underlying database can be found in the Annex 12.b and in [1-3]. A decision on whether
to use specific source data is dictated by the limitations of the different i nput methods found within the
Annex of the respective test method (TG 442C, TG 442D and TG 442E). At least 2 me thods that cover 2
key events should be used as input data.
111. The correlation of individual information sources and their combination to se nsitiser potency in the
LLNA has been analysed in the literature [9]. The stability of the regression model s on different datasets
have been analysed in detail, indicating a high robustness of the regression -based models [1, 2] . The
consistency of the result when using three or only two information sources was investigated in s upporting
file ESM3 to [1], which is accessible under 10.14573/altex.2201141. The performance of the individual
regression models was shown as summary statistics in Table 2 in [1] and in Table 4 in [3], and for individual
chemicals in the file ESM1 to [1] accessible under 10.14573/altex.2201141. A high consistency of
predictions was also observed if the models were trained on LLNA EC3 only or on PV, with a lower
importance of cytotoxicity and a higher contribution of cellular activation markers for models trained on PV
[3] (see Table 4 in [3]). The uncertainty in predicting in vivo data using these models should also be viewed
in the context of the inherent variability of human and animal reference data and the c orrelation between
these data, see e.g. [10].
4.2.5 Proficiency Chemicals
112. The regression models use a fixed data interpretation procedure to derive the PoD. Proficiency
chemicals for the individual in chemico and in vitro information sources (KE1, KE2, KE3) are defined in the
respective guidelines (OECD TG 442C, 442D, 442E) ([2,4,5]). The details to apply the regres sion models
are directly included in the Spreadsheet, which forms Annex 12.b of the Supporting Document to this
guideline. Proficiency for the individual information sources demonstrates proficiency for the DA.
4.2.6 Predictive Capacity of the regression-based DA
113. The regression-based DA derives a PoD for risk assessment. The model estimates the dose of
the EC3 value in the LLNA or the dose at which skin sensitisation is likely to occur in 4% of a HPPT-eligible
human population (DSA04 value). DSA04 value in µg/cm 2 are correlated to EC3 values expressed in
µg/cm2 and both values represent the lower end of the dose-response curve for experimental indu ction of
skin sensitization. These values are combined in the PV [3, 4]. The P oD is therefore defined as a best
estimate for either the LLNA EC3 or the WoE PV. PoDs were computed for 220 chemicals listed in Annex
4.2.A. The PoDs were compared to reference EC3 values or PV. When evaluatin g the PoD vs. the LLNA
EC3 MLLP in the DASS database (n=146), 126/146 (86%) of regression-based PoDs are within 10-fold of
the reference value, with 8/146 (5.5%) having a > 10-fold underpredicted potency. Furthermore, 59/146
(40%) of the PoDs are within 2-fold of the reference value. When the PoD are compared to the LLNA EC3
in the full database (n=220; including those EC3 values non-evaluated or exc luded by the DASS review),
a similar result is obtained: 191/220 (87%) of regression- based PoDs are within 10-fold of the reference
value, with 13/220 (6.3%) having a > 10-fold underpredicted potency. Furthermore, 80/220 (36%) of the
PoDs are within 2-fold of the reference value. The same PoDs were compared to the PV (n=139). 120/139
(86%) of PoDs are within 10-fold of the reference value, with 12/139 (8.9%) having a > 10-fold
underpredicted potency. Furthermore, 43/139 (31%) of PoDs are within 2-fold of the reference value .
Regression-based PoDs give a balanced prediction relative to the chosen reference v alues (geometric
mean fold-differences vs. LLNA is 0.86 and vs. PV it is 0.99). Further analyses are made in Annex 12.c in
the Supporting Document of this guideline [ 11]. Figure 4.4 shows regression-based PoDs compared to
reference LLNA MLLPs in the DASS evaluation database.

4.2.7 Reporting of the DA
114. The reporting of the regression-based DA should follow the template described in OECD GD 255
(6), and should include at a minimum the following elements:
• Test chemical identification ( e.g. chemical name, structural formula, composition, isomers,
impurities including their quantities as available, CAS number, batch and lot nu mber, and other
relevant identifiers)
• Individual test reports including raw data for the individual tests performed per corresponding
guideline (OECD TG 442C, 442D, 442E). Note that the chemical identity for each test report should
match that above.
• A copy of the prediction spreadsheet with input data and results
• Outcome of the DA application: Point of departure derived, indication on which regression equation
and information sources the PoD is based on
• Assessment whether the chemical is in the applicability domain of the indivi dual information
sources
• Any deviation from the regression-based DA
• Conclusion

section_title: Introduction
content:
116. As described in Section 3.1, the ITS defined approach (DA) are based on three information
sources: an in chemico assay (DPRA, ADRA, TG 442C) (1), an in vitro assay (h-CLAT, U-SENS ™,
GARD®Skin, TG 442E) (2), and one in silico method (Derek Nexus or OECD Toolbox) prediction from the
models listed in Appendices I- II of this guideline (referred to hereafter as in silico )) (3-4). For each
information source a score is given depending on the outcome of the individual assay and/or prediction, that
is then summed to obtain the DA prediction (5).
Applicability domain of the individual information sources
In chemico/in vitro information source
117. A test chemical is considered to be within the in chemico/in vitro information source domain (i.e.
applicable) if it can be tested according to the individual protocols, takin g into account the technical and
chemical type limitations of each assay (as defined in the respective TGs (442C and 442E (1, 2)). The in
chemico/in vitro results are considered applicable, in case there are no technical or chemical space specific
limitations and no reason why the results obtained from the assay cannot be considered.
In silico information source
118. The ITS DAs use in silico information sources that are based on chemical structures. These in
silico sources rely on molecular representation of the chemicals: input usually by drawin g the chemical
structure, or by entering the Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES) or the IUPAC
International Chemical Identifier (InChi). A test chemical is considered to be within the in silico information
source domain if it is a single chemical (i.e. mixtures and UVCBs are outside the applicability domain) and
a prediction can be made, taking into account the individual applicability doma in of the in silico model (as
defined in Appendix I-II). As a single chemical can be represented by several CAS or EC numbers (due to
differences in composition, e.g. stereochemical differences, present as varied salt forms, present as the
main component in a mixture), it is important to specify the exact structure. Resources s uch as the US
EPA CompTox Chemicals Dashboard ( https://comptox.epa.gov/dashboard) or NIH PubChem
(https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) may be useful in mapping chemical names or structures to SMILES or
InChi format. Available guidance can be consulted regarding minimum purity lev el of substances used in
in silico predictions based on molecular structure.1718
Confidence in ITS predictions
119. The applicability domain of the individual information sources used in the ITS DA are assessed and
this determines whether the ITS predictions can be considered conclusive (i.e. high confidence) or
inconclusive (i.e. low confidence) for hazard identification and/or potency.
How to apply the data interpretation procedure (DIP) for the ITS
120. The ITS uses three information sources based on in chemico (KE1) (1) and in vitro (KE3) data (2),
and an in silico prediction (3), with a DIP developed with EG DASS input. Where all three information
sources are applicable, a conclusive ITS prediction can be made. In some cases, a conclusive ITS prediction
can be made, if there are only two information sources with applicable results ( Figure A2.1).
17 OECD (2017), Guidance on Grouping of Chemicals, Second Editi on, OECD Series on Testing and Assessment,
No. 194, OECD Publishing, Paris, https://doi.org/10.1787/9789264274679-en.
18 ECHA (2008) CHAPTER R.6 – QSARS AND GROUPING OF CHEMICALS in Guidance on
Information Requirements and Chemical Safety Assessment. European Chemicals Agency [Guidance on Information
Requirements and Chemical Safety Assessment - ECHA (europa.eu)

Note: The ITS defined approach (DA) are based on three information sources: an in chem ico assay (DPRA, ADRA, TG 442C) (1), an in vitro
assay (h-CLAT, U-SENS™, GARD®Skin, TG 442E) (2), and one in silico method (Derek Nexus or OECD Toolbox prediction from the models
listed in Appendices I-II of this guideline) (3-4). For each information source a score is given depending on the outcome of the individual assay
and/or prediction, that is then summed to obtain the DA prediction. Scoring information can be found in Table 3.1.
121. Depending on the applicability of the individual information sources, three di fferent scenarios for
the ITS DA are possible (see Appendices I-II, Annex 2 Figure A 2.1. and Annex 2 Table A 2.1. ). In
Scenario 1, all three information sources are applicable. In Scenarios 2 and 3, only two information sources
are applicable. Details are provided below:
122. Scenario 1: all of the information sources i.e. in chemico/in vitro outcomes are applicable and can
be considered (as prescribed in each individual assay) and the in silico prediction is in domain. The
obtained ITS DA prediction is conclusive and of high confidence
123. Scenario 2: in silico prediction out of domain, however in chemico/in vitro methods are in domain
and provide conclusive predictions (i.e. in chemico/in vitro methods are applicable).
• Combined DA score of 0, 2, 3, 4 or 6, in silico prediction out of in silico domain: DA conclusion is
possible based on the two in chemico/in vitro outcomes. Conclusive prediction as the in silico
prediction would not lead to a different DA prediction.
• Combined DA score of 5, in silico prediction out of in silico domain: DA conclusion possible for
hazard identification (conclusive positive DA prediction for hazard identification). DA conclusion not
possible for potency (inconclusive DA prediction for potency).
• Combined DA score of 1, in silico prediction out of in silico domain: DA conclusion not possible.
Inconclusive DA prediction for hazard identification and potency.
124. Scenario 3: one in chemico/in vitro method out of domain or the result of that method cannot be
considered (inapplicable):
• Combined DA score of 2 based on one in chemico/in vitro and in silico prediction: DA conclusion
possible. Conclusive DA prediction as UN GHS 1B, as the outcome of the other in chemico/in vitro
method would not lead to a different DA prediction.
• Combined DA score of 3 or 4, based on one in chemico/in vitro and in silico prediction: DA
conclusion possible for hazard identification (conclusive positive DA predi ction for hazard
identification). DA conclusion not possible for potency (inconclusive DA prediction fo r potency).
• Combined DA score of 0 or 1, one in chemico/in vitro and in silico prediction: DA conclusion not
possible. Inconclusive prediction for hazard identification and potency.
