Description of Derek Nexus
125. Derek is an expert, knowledge-based software tool comprising alerts on several toxicity endpoints,
including skin sensitisation. Derek fires alerts based on structural features, i.e. whether a hapten has
potential for electrophilic binding to skin proteins either directly or following me tabolism/auto-oxidation
(1). Additional information on this model can be found in the QSAR Model Reporting Format (QMRF) (2).
Applicability domain of Derek Nexus
126. To each skin sensitisation alert, a likelihood level is associated. Chemica ls firing an alert with a
likelihood of certain, probable, plausible, or equivocal are considered to be positi ve. Chemicals with a
negative prediction of ‘non -sensitiser with no mis classified or unclassified features’ are considered to be
negative.
127. Skin sensitisation predictions from Derek Nexus v6.1.0 are used in the ITS DA. All po sitive
predictions (likelihood = certain, probable, plausible or equivocal) are considered to be inside the
applicability domain. Negative predictions (likelihood = doubted, improbable, impossible or non-sensitiser)
are also considered to be in the applicability domain unless they contain misclas sified and/or unclassified
features. A prediction of non-sensitiser with misclassified features indicates th e presence of a fragment
that has been observed exclusively in known sensitisers which Derek fails to alert for. A prediction of non-
sensitiser with unclassified features indicates the presence of a fragment that has no t been observed in
publicly available data (although Derek may have seen this in proprietary data) (3). Usually, expert review
is recommended for predictions containing these features but as a fixed data i nterpretation procedure,
required in a DA, does not permit expert review these are best considered as out of domain for use in the

Description of OECD QSAR Toolbox
129. The OECD QSAR Toolbox is a freely available software application that suppo rts reproducible and
transparent chemical hazard assessment. It offers functionalities for retrieving experi mental data,
simulating metabolism and profiling properties of chemicals. These information and tools can be used to
find structurally and mechanistically defined analogues and chemical categor ies, which can serve as
sources for read-across and trend analysis for data gap filling (1)]. Add itional information on this model
can be found in the QSAR Model Reporting Format (QMRF) (2).
Applicability domain of OECD QSAR Toolbox
Technical aspects
130. The Toolbox prediction used by the DA ITS is calculated using the DASS automated workflow
(DASS AW) included in OECD QSAR Toolbox v.4.5. The workflow also includes the automatic calculation
of the applicability domain.
Calculation of the in silico domain of Toolbox
131. Applicability domain of the QSAR Toolbox Skin sensitisation predictions for use in the ITS defined
approach automated workflow (DASS AW) is defined by based on the training set substances of the same
automated workflow. The training set (TS) consists of 2268 substances having LLNA and/or GPMT skin
sensitisation experimental data 20 (the full list of substances can be consulted in the QSAR Toolbox). The
TS substances are part of the following OECD QSAR Toolbox databases:
1. Skin sensitisation;
2. REACH Skin sensitisation (normalized) databases.
132. Based on the correctly predicted training set substances, three layers of applicability domain are
automatically calculated by the Toolbox: 1) parametric; 2) structural and 3) mechanistic layers. Depending
on the Toolbox prediction approach (read-across or profiling predictions) and prediction outcomes (positive
or negative), one or more of these layers are taken into account to establish the overall Toolbox domain of
the specific prediction.
20 In case of multiple data points for one substance, the most conservative scenario is taken into account.
133. The applicability domain layers considered for different types of Toolbox pr edictions are
summarised in the table here:
Toolbox DASS
AW outcome
Applicability domain layer
Structural Parametric Mechanistic
Positive Read-across Not considered Not considered Considered
Profiling Not considered Not considered Met by definition
Negative Read-across Not considered Not considered Considered
Profiling Considered Considered Met by definition
134. Explanation and rationale for the use of different domain layers:
1. Positive predictions (both by read-across and profiling): the presence of an al ert (which is the
requirement for positive Toolbox prediction to be considered within in the mec hanistic domain) is
sufficient to consider the prediction to be within the Toolbox domain. Substances triggering an alert
are considered as in domain because they contain the toxicophore that has been observed
experimentally in skin sensitisers. No further checks are needed in this co ntext to consider the
prediction within the Toolbox in silico domain.
2. Negative predictions by read-across: the structural and parametric domains are n ot taken into
account because the Toolbox has already ensured some level of similarity with other substances
in its training set that met the requirements to be selected as suitable analo gues for read-across
(these requirements are explained in detail in the DASS AW description).
3. Negative prediction by profiling predictions: all domain layers are taken into account to ensure the
highest possible reliability level for the Toolbox prediction. Stricter requirements are needed mainly
for two reasons: 1. lack of alerts is not equal to proof of lack of sensitisation potential and 2. to
apply a cautious approach since acceptance of negative predictions may lower the human health
protection level risk in case of a false negative predictions.
Calculation of applicability domain layers
1. Parametric layer
Four physicochemical parameters of the substances are taken into consideration: log Kow, molecular
weight, vapour pressure and water solubility 21. The ranges of variation for the selected parameters are
defined based on the training set substances that are correctly predicted by the DASS AW.
A substance is considered within the parametric domain of the DASS AW if its physicochemical parameter
values as calculated by the QSAR Toolbox fall into the ranges of variation given in the table below. It is
noted that the ranges include parametric values calculated using EPISuite models implemented in Toolbox
that in some cases are wider than that covered by existing test methods.
Physicochemical

2. Structural layer
The structural layer is defined based on the atom centred fragments (ACF) derived from the structural
characteristics of the TS substances that are correctly predicted 22 by the DASS AW.
The ACF are defined according to the following Toolbox default values for ACF:
• Any atom distance = 1
• Heteroatom distance = 1
• Extract C (sp 3) fragments = YES
• Include whole aromatic rings = NO
For each substance, the following values are calculated:
• % Correct fragments: percentage of ACF occurring in correctly predicted structures in the trai ning
set
• % incorrect fragments: percentage of ACF occurring in incorrectly predicted s tructures in the
training set
• % unknown fragments: percentage of ACF not occurring in the training set.
A substance is considered within the structural domain of the DASS AW if 100% o f its ACF belong to the
correct fragments.
3. Mechanistic layer
The predicted capability of a substance to interact with the skin proteins without and af ter (a)biotic
activation is taken into consideration. The Toolbox endpoint-specific profiler Protein binding for skin
sensitization by OASIS and two metabolic simulators – Autoxidation simulator and Skin metabolism
simulator are used to predict such interaction.
A positive prediction is considered within the mechanistic domain if the s ubstance triggers alerts from the
profiler “ Protein binding for skin sensitization by OASIS ” without or after (a)biotic activation.
A negative prediction is considered within the mechanistic domain if the s ubstance does not trigger alerts
from the profiler “Protein binding for skin sensitization by OASIS” without or after (a)biotic activation.
Note that predictions obtained by profiling results will meet the mechanistic layer requirements by definition
because positive Toolbox predictions by profiler are triggered exactly by the presence of alert. If the test

Protocol for generating predictions for skin sensitisation hazard using DASS AW in Toolbox 4.5.
135. The following protocol should be used to generate predictions for skin sensit isation hazard using
OECD QSAR Toolbox v.4.5 with the automated workflow for defined approaches for skin sen sitisation
(DASS AW) to be used as the in silico information source for the ITSv2 defined approach.
Step 1 : Input the chemical in the “Input module”. SMILES is the preferred way to input the
structure. (If other identifiers such as the CAS number are used as input, the Toolbox will assign
the SMILES based on its internal database. In this case, the user needs to make sure that Toolbox
identifies and consequently uses for the prediction the correct structure.)
Step 2: Go to the “Data gap filling module” and click on “Automated” button. Select “EC3 from

workflow will run automatically.
Step 4 : If a substance is predicted “positive” or “negative” as a result of read -across, the

section_title: Appendix III: Protocol for Generating SARA-ICE
content:
Predictions
The following protocol should be used to generate predictions for point of departur e for skin sensitisation
risk assessment using SARA-ICE DA v.1.0.
1. Establishing SARA-ICE Inputs
1. Click ‘Download Template’
An example template is available if needed. Click ‘Download Example’.
A key is provided on the final tab.
2. Select ‘Substances’ tab. Add distinct chemical substances (1 or more).
a. Input name for the chemical(s) in column A ‘Substance Name’
b. Optional: Add an abbreviated/shorter substance name that will appear in tables, figures
etc. in column B ‘Abbreviated Substance Name’.
If this is not used the tool will automatically revert to the substance name in column A .
c. Input CAS number (or other unique identifier) in column C
Whichever unique identifier is used here will also be used within the data tabs to ensure
data for this chemical is linked across data types
d. Input Molecular weight (MW) in g/mol, in column D, if using kDPRA and/or KeratinoSens
data inputs. This allows automatic conversion from molar to mass concentrations.
3. Populate data tabs
Although the model can technically be run with no chemical specific information (in which case the resulting
ED01 estimates will be taken directly from the prior distribution), any inputted c hemical specific data will
inform the ED 01 distribution. A minimum of 2 test methods per compound, covering minimum of two key
events, should be entered into the data template as per the guideline to ensure ad equate uncertainty
reduction in the ED01 distribution. Reference methods which can be used as SARA-ICE DA inputs include:
the Direct Peptide Reactivity Assay (DPRA; OECD TG 442C), kinetic DPRA (kDPRA; OECD TG 442C),
KeratinoSens (OECD TG 442D), the human cell line activation test (h-CLAT; OECD T G 442E), and U-
SENS (OECD TG 442E), as well as in vivo methods such as the local lymp h node assay (LLNA; OECD
TG 429, OECD TG 442A, OECD TG 442B) and HPPT test methods human repeat insult patch tests and
human maximization tests. No new in vivo data should be produced for use in SARA-ICE DA.
a. HPPT
i. Optional: Input ‘Substance Name’ in column A
ii. Input CAS number (or other chosen unique identifier) in column B
Whichever unique identifier is used here will also be used within the d ata tabs to
ensure data for this chemical is linked across data types
iii. Input dose per skin area (µg/cm 2) in column C
iv. Input number of test subjects in column D
v. Input number of test subjects with positive sensitisation responses (post
elicitation phase of the HPPT study) in column E
vi. Optional: Input data source reference in column F
Note, this is not used within the model but will be included in output reports
b. LLNA
i. Optional: Input ‘Substance Name’ in column A
ii. Input CAS number (or other chosen unique identifier) in column B
Whichever unique identifier is used here will also be used within the d ata tabs to
ensure data for this chemical is linked across data types
iii. Input the (estimated) EC3 (%) in column C
Negative studies should be entered as >X where X is the maximum concentration
tested. Studies were the SI > 3 at the lowest reported/tested concentration should
be entered as <X where X is the lowest concentration reported/tested.
iv. Optional: Input data source reference in column D
Note, this is not used within the model but will be included in output reports
c. DPRA
i. Optional: Input ‘Substance Name’ in column A
ii. Input CAS number (or other chosen unique identifier) in column B
Whichever unique identifier is used here will also be used within the d ata tabs to
ensure data for this chemical is linked across data types
iii. Input percentage depletion of the cysteine peptide in column C
iv. Input percentage depletion of the lysine peptide in column D
v. Optional: Input data source reference in column E
Note, this is not used within the model but will be included in output reports
d. kDPRA
i. Optional: Input ‘Substance Name’ in column A
ii. Input CAS number (or other chosen unique identifier) in column B
Whichever unique identifier is used here will also be used within the d ata tabs to
ensure data for this chemical is linked across data types
iii. Input log Kmax value in column C
When reactivity rate is too low to measure, input as <X where X is the lowest
possible measurable reactivity rate. Typically X=-3.5 M -1 s-1
iv. Optional: Input data source reference in column D
Note, this is not used within the model but will be included in output reports
e. KeratinoSens TM
i. Optional: Input ‘Substance Name’ in column A
ii. Input CAS number (or other chosen unique identifier) in column B
Whichever unique identifier is used here will also be used within the d ata tabs to
ensure data for this chemical is linked across data types
iii. Input EC1.5 (µM) (concentration resulting in a 1.5-fold increase in luciferase
activity) in column C
iv. Input IC50 (µM) (concentration resulting in 50% cell death in the KeratinoSens
study) in column D
v. Optional: Input data source reference in column E
Note, this is not used within the model but will be included in output reports
f. h-CLAT
i. Optional: Input ‘Substance Name’ in column A
ii. Input CAS number (or other chosen unique identifier) in column B
Whichever unique identifier is used here will also be used within the d ata tabs to
ensure data for this chemical is linked across data types
iii. Input CD54 EC200 (µg/ml) in column C
Concentration resulting in a 200% increase in expression of the CD54 biomarker.
Input can be entered as >X where X is the maximum concentration tested if not
concentration-dependent response is observed in the assay. If a biomarker shows
a response at the minimum tested concentration, input result as <X where X is the
minimum concentration tested.
iv. Input CD86 EC150 (µg/ml) in column D
Concentration resulting in a 150% increase in expression of the CD86 biomarker.
Input can be entered as >X where X is the maximum concentration tested if not
concentration-dependent response is observed in the assay. If a biomarker shows
a response at the minimum tested concentration, input result as <X where X is the
minimum concentration tested.
v. Input CV75 (µg/ml) in column E
Concentration at which there is 75% cell viability.
vi. Optional: Input data source reference in column F
Note, this is not used within the model but will be included in output reports
g. USENS TM
i. Optional: Input ‘Substance Name’ in column A
ii. Input CAS number (or other chosen unique identifier) in column B
Whichever unique identifier is used here will also be used within the d ata tabs to
ensure data for this chemical is linked across data types
iii. Input EC150 (µg/ml) in column C
Concentration resulting in a 150% increase in expression of the CD86 biomarker.
Input can be entered as >X where X is the maximum concentration tested if not
concentration-dependent response is observed in the assay. If a biomarker shows
a response at the minimum tested concentration, input result as <X where X is the
minimum concentration tested.
iv. Input CV70 (µg/ml) in column D
Concentration at which there is 70% cell viability
v. Optional: Input data source reference in column E
Note, this is not used within the model but will be included in output reports
4. Save completed template file
2. Running the SARA-ICE Model
1. Click ‘Choose input’ on the SARA-ICE DA user interface
2. Select saved completed template file
3. Click ‘Run Analysis’
Running the model involves drawing samples from the posterior distribution using the No-U-
Turn sampler implemented within the probabilistic programming language Stan. By defau lt, a
sample of 10,000 draws of the ED 01 is returned to the user. Summary statistics such as
quantile estimates of the distribution are calculated empirically on this sample.
The No-U-Turn sampler produces a Markov Chain whose stationary distribution is th e
posterior distribution of the model. A successful model run is achieved when the Markov Chain
converges to the target distribution. The Stan software provides several measures of
convergence to assess whether convergence may be assumed.
3. SARA-ICE Model Outputs
1. The 5 th, 50 th and 95 th percentiles of the ED 01 (µg cm -2) are provided in tabular format and the
prediction interval is presented in a graphical format within the user interface.
These data are also available within a downloadable template format (.xlsx or .csv), click ‘Download
Analysis’ for the appropriate file format . The downloadable template also provides the ED 01 at all
percentiles ranging from 0.5 th to 95.5th (in 0.5 increments). This template also provides the full set
of draws from which summary statistics are computed.
2. The SARA-ICE PoD (computed as the geometric mean of the ED 01 distribution conditional on it
being less than 60,000 µg cm-2) is provided in a tabular format within the user interface.
A conservative PoD (calculated at the 5 th percentile of the ED01 conditional on it being less than
60,000 µg cm-2 is also provided and these data are also available within a downloadable template
format (.xlsx or .csv), click ‘Download Analysis’ for the appropriate file format.
3. The SARA-ICE probability of binary (S/NC) and GHS subcategory (1A, 1B, NC) are gi ven in a
tabular format within the user interface.
Note, this is a capability of the SARA-ICE model shared through the user inter face but does not
form part of the SARA-ICE DA within OECD TG 497. These data are also available within a
downloadable template format (.xlsx or .csv), click ‘Download Analysis’ for the ap propriate file
format.
4. The SARA-ICE GHS category call is provided in a tabular format within the user interface. T he
classification is dependent on the confidence in the prediction, e.g., a probabi lity threshold. The
probability threshold for a high-confidence prediction must be higher than the prior probability of
0.67. Sliders within the user interface are provided to the user in order to set the proba bility
threshold as per their requirements.
Note, this is a capability of the SARA-ICE model shared through the user inter face but does not
form part of the SARA-ICE DA within OECD TG 497. A full sensitivity analys is on the impact of
varying the probability threshold can be found in supporting documentation. The se data are also
available within a downloadable template format (.xlsx or .csv), click ‘Down load Analysis’ for the
appropriate file format.
